items.stem: Which of the following best describes "evidence"?
options: The art of persuasive speaking or writing
A regular article in which a writer argues a personal view on a topical issue
Facts, statistics, examples, expert opinion or anecdotes that support a claim
The main point or position an argument sets out to prove
items.answer: Facts, statistics, examples, expert opinion or anecdotes that support a claim
items.markingKey: C. "evidence" is facts, statistics, examples, expert opinion or anecdotes that support a claim.

items.stem:
Read the following opinion column in a youth news magazine.

Let Us Vote at 16
At 16 I can work, pay tax on my wages and, in some countries, join the army. But I can't vote for the people who decide how that tax is spent.
Critics say teenagers are too immature. Yet Austria has let 16-year-olds vote in national elections since 2007, and studies there found young voters were just as informed as older first-time voters.
Climate, housing, education – the decisions made today will shape our lives for longer than anyone's.
We are not asking for a favour. We are asking for a voice.

Identify the claim, evidence, counterargument and rebuttal in this text.
items.answer: Claim: the voting age should be lowered to 16. Evidence: 16-year-olds can work and pay tax; Austria's experience since 2007 suggests young voters are well informed. Counterargument: critics say teenagers are immature. Rebuttal: the Austrian studies, and the point that young people will live longest with today's decisions.
items.markingKey: Claim: the voting age should be lowered to 16. Evidence: 16-year-olds can work and pay tax; Austria's experience since 2007 suggests young voters are well informed. Counterargument: critics say teenagers are immature. Rebuttal: the Austrian studies, and the point that young people will live longest with today's decisions. Award marks for an accurate, specific point supported by a reference to the text (criterion A). A general assertion without evidence earns at most 1 mark.

items.stem: Explain the difference between a rebuttal and a counterargument.
items.answer: A counterargument states the opposing view; a rebuttal answers it, showing why it is weaker or wrong.
items.markingKey: A counterargument states the opposing view; a rebuttal answers it, showing why it is weaker or wrong. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A student claims: "Mentioning the other side weakens your argument." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Acknowledging and rebutting the other side strengthens your argument by showing fairness and anticipating objections.
items.markingKey: Acknowledging and rebutting the other side strengthens your argument by showing fairness and anticipating objections. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Read the following speech by a student council president to her school assembly in Toronto.

Good morning, everyone. Raise your hand if you checked your phone before breakfast today. (Pause.) Me too.
We are the most connected generation in history – and, according to our own school survey, 62 per cent of us say we feel lonely every week. Connected, but alone.
I'm not asking you to throw your phone in the lake. I'm asking for one hour. One lunchtime a week, phones in our bags, eyes on each other.
Let's try it. Let's talk. Let's remember what our friends' faces look like when they laugh.

Explain how the humorous concession "I'm not asking you to throw your phone in the lake" contributes to the meaning of the text.
items.answer: The humorous concession "I'm not asking you to throw your phone in the lake": it anticipates an objection and makes the actual request seem small and reasonable.
items.markingKey: The humorous concession "I'm not asking you to throw your phone in the lake": it anticipates an objection and makes the actual request seem small and reasonable. Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature or technique, a precise quotation or reference, and an explanation of its effect on the reader linked to the writer's purpose (criterion A). Naming a feature without explaining its effect: half marks at most.

items.stem: Write a claim, one piece of evidence, a counterargument and a rebuttal for the topic "Schools should start at 10 a.m."
items.answer: Claim: schools should start at 10 a.m. Evidence: research on teenage sleep cycles. Counterargument: it would disrupt parents' work schedules. Rebuttal: flexible drop-off schemes and improved learning outweigh the inconvenience. 1 mark each.
items.markingKey: Claim: schools should start at 10 a.m. Evidence: research on teenage sleep cycles. Counterargument: it would disrupt parents' work schedules. Rebuttal: flexible drop-off schemes and improved learning outweigh the inconvenience. 1 mark each.

Let's try it. Let's talk. Let's remember what our friends' faces look like when they laugh.

How does the speaker persuade her audience to try a phone-free lunchtime?
Write one analytical paragraph (point, evidence, explanation) that answers this question, using at least two quotations.
items.answer: The speaker builds trust before persuading: the opening show of hands and "Me too" make the habit shared, not shameful (ethos). The school statistic and the paradox "Connected, but alone" give logical and emotional weight. The humorous concession shrinks the request to "one hour", and the anaphoric "Let's..." ending turns agreement into collective action, closing on the emotive image of friends laughing.

The school statistic and the paradox "Connected, but alone" give logical and emotional weight. Mark mainly against criterion A (Analysing) and B (Organising). 7-8 equivalent: perceptive analysis of how specific choices create effects, well-chosen embedded evidence, sustained, logical structure; 5-6: substantial analysis with relevant evidence; 3-4: adequate, partly descriptive; 1-2: limited, mostly feature-spotting or retelling.

items.stem: Briefly explain why including a counterargument can make an argument stronger.
items.answer: It shows the writer has considered other views and allows them to answer objections before the reader raises them, building trust.

items.stem: Freya writes: "The more statistics you use, the more persuasive your argument." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Too many statistics can overwhelm; well-chosen evidence, clearly explained, is more persuasive.

items.stem:
Read the following opinion column by a teacher in a school newsletter.

Less Homework, Better Learning?
I have set homework for twenty years. I now think I set too much.
Research from several countries suggests that, for students your age, the benefits of homework level off after about an hour or two a night. Beyond that, sleep, exercise and family time matter more.
Some parents worry that less homework means lower standards. I understand. But a tired student who copies answers at midnight learns nothing.
So this term, my classes will get less homework – and better homework.

Identify the claim, evidence, counterargument and rebuttal in this text.
items.answer: Claim: students should get less but better homework. Evidence: research showing benefits level off after one to two hours. Counterargument: parents fear lower standards. Rebuttal: an exhausted student copying answers learns nothing.
items.markingKey: Claim: students should get less but better homework. Evidence: research showing benefits level off after one to two hours. Counterargument: parents fear lower standards. Rebuttal: an exhausted student copying answers learns nothing. Award marks for an accurate, specific point supported by a reference to the text (criterion A). A general assertion without evidence earns at most 1 mark.

items.stem: "An argument with emotional appeal is more effective than one based on logic." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: The most effective arguments combine sound logic with emotional engagement, adapted to the audience.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: emotion motivates action; stories are memorable. Arguments against: logic builds trust and withstands scrutiny; emotional manipulation can backfire. Supported judgement: The most effective arguments combine sound logic with emotional engagement, adapted to the audience. Markbands (12 marks): MYP criteria (each 0-8, scaled to this item). A Analysing: explains content, context, language, structure, technique and style and their effects; justifies opinions with examples and explanation, using terminology. B Organising: a clear, logical structure suited to the task; ideas linked with purpose; referencing conventions. C Producing text: insight, imagination and personal engagement; deliberate stylistic choices; relevant detail and examples. D Using language: varied, accurate vocabulary, sentence structures and forms of expression; appropriate register and style; accurate grammar, spelling and punctuation. 7-8 perceptive/excellent; 5-6 substantial; 3-4 adequate; 1-2 limited.

items.stem: "I have set homework for twenty years." Which appeal is this?
items.answer: Ethos
items.markingKey: Ethos. Experience builds credibility.

items.stem: Explain the difference between logos and pathos.
items.answer: Pathos persuades through emotion (images of suffering, hope); logos persuades through reason and evidence (statistics, logical consequences).
items.markingKey: Pathos persuades through emotion (images of suffering, hope); logos persuades through reason and evidence (statistics, logical consequences). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: "Pathos is a dishonest way to persuade." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Emotional appeals are legitimate when they are relevant and truthful; they become manipulative only when they distort or replace evidence.
items.markingKey: Emotional appeals are legitimate when they are relevant and truthful; they become manipulative only when they distort or replace evidence. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Read the following opinion column by a Year 10 student in a school magazine in Melbourne.

Why I've Changed My Mind About Uniforms
In Year 7 I thought school uniform was a prison sentence in polyester. I wanted to wear my own clothes, my own style, my own identity.
Then I met Jonah. Jonah's family couldn't afford the brands everyone else wore. On mufti days he 'forgot' and wore his blazer anyway.
A uniform doesn't erase who we are. It erases the price tag.
Yes, the jumpers are itchy. Yes, the colour is a crime against fashion. But I'd rather be itchy than watch a friend hide.

State the main purpose of the text and explain how one feature helps to achieve it.
items.answer: To persuade readers that school uniform protects less wealthy students from being judged. Supporting evidence: "a prison sentence in polyester" (metaphor) – the exaggerated image humorously captures how restrictive uniform felt, and the alliteration makes it memorable.
items.markingKey: To persuade readers that school uniform protects less wealthy students from being judged. Supporting evidence: "a prison sentence in polyester" (metaphor) – the exaggerated image humorously captures how restrictive uniform felt, and the alliteration makes it memorable. Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature or technique, a precise quotation or reference, and an explanation of its effect on the reader linked to the writer's purpose (criterion A). Naming a feature without explaining its effect: half marks at most.

items.stem: Write one sentence using each appeal (ethos, pathos, logos) to persuade students to join a litter-picking club.
items.answer: Ethos: "As captain of the eco-club for two years, I have seen what we can achieve." Pathos: "Imagine a turtle tangled in a crisp packet you dropped." Logos: "Last term we collected 400 kg of litter in four hours."

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "Logos is the most important rhetorical appeal."
items.answer: Logos is essential, but its impact depends on the speaker's credibility and on emotional engagement; the appeals work best together.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: evidence makes an argument credible; it withstands scrutiny. Arguments against: audiences act on emotion; without ethos the evidence may not be trusted. Supported judgement: Logos is essential, but its impact depends on the speaker's credibility and on emotional engagement; the appeals work best together.

items.stem:
Read the following letter from a student to her local council in Manchester.

Dear Councillor Patel,
I am writing to ask you to reconsider the decision to close Levenshulme Library.
For many students in my area, the library is the only quiet place to study. My flat has five people and one table. The library has Wi-Fi, printers and Mrs Okafor, who has helped me with every homework project since I was eight.
Closing it would save money this year, but it would cost our community far more in the future.
I would be grateful if you could meet our youth group to discuss alternatives.
Yours sincerely,
Amira Hassan (age 14)

Who is the target audience of the text? Refer to two details that suggest this audience.
items.answer: A local councillor who has power over the decision; the formal salutation and polite requests suit this official audience. Supporting evidence: "I would be grateful if you could meet our youth group" (formal register) – polite, formal language shows respect and makes the request hard to refuse.
items.markingKey: A local councillor who has power over the decision; the formal salutation and polite requests suit this official audience. Supporting evidence: "I would be grateful if you could meet our youth group" (formal register) – polite, formal language shows respect and makes the request hard to refuse. Award marks for an accurate, specific point supported by a reference to the text (criterion A). A general assertion without evidence earns at most 1 mark.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "Humour makes an opinion column more persuasive."
items.answer: Humour can be very persuasive when it supports, rather than replaces, a serious argument, as in the uniform column.

items.answer: The explanation of how the evidence supports the claim
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the explanation of how the evidence supports the claim. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Define the term "ethos".
items.answer: An appeal to the speaker's or writer's credibility, character or authority
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: an appeal to the speaker's or writer's credibility, character or authority. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain the difference between an editorial and an opinion column.
items.answer: An opinion column expresses an individual writer's view under their name; an editorial expresses the official view of the publication.
items.markingKey: An opinion column expresses an individual writer's view under their name; an editorial expresses the official view of the publication. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: "Mentioning the other side weakens your argument." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Acknowledging and rebutting the other side strengthens your argument by showing fairness and anticipating objections.
items.markingKey: Acknowledging and rebutting the other side strengthens your argument by showing fairness and anticipating objections. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between logos and pathos.
items.answer: Pathos persuades through emotion (images of suffering, hope); logos persuades through reason and evidence (statistics, logical consequences).
items.markingKey: Pathos persuades through emotion (images of suffering, hope); logos persuades through reason and evidence (statistics, logical consequences). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem:
Read the following opinion column by a teacher in a school newsletter.

Less Homework, Better Learning?
I have set homework for twenty years. I now think I set too much.
Research from several countries suggests that, for students your age, the benefits of homework level off after about an hour or two a night. Beyond that, sleep, exercise and family time matter more.
Some parents worry that less homework means lower standards. I understand. But a tired student who copies answers at midnight learns nothing.
So this term, my classes will get less homework – and better homework.

Outline the conventions of the text type used here, with examples from the extract.
items.answer: It is a opinion column. Conventions: a by-line, a first-person argument on a topical issue, evidence and anecdote, a counterargument and a clear stance. In this text, for example: "I have set homework for twenty years. I now think I set too much." (ethos (experience and honesty)), each chosen to suit the purpose and audience.
items.markingKey: It is a opinion column. Conventions: a by-line, a first-person argument on a topical issue, evidence and anecdote, a counterargument and a clear stance. In this text, for example: "I have set homework for twenty years. I now think I set too much." (ethos (experience and honesty)), each chosen to suit the purpose and audience. Award marks for an accurate, specific point supported by a reference to the text (criterion A). A general assertion without evidence earns at most 1 mark.

items.stem: Explain the difference between evidence and a claim.
items.answer: A claim is the position being argued ("the voting age should be 16"); evidence is the support for it (Austria's experience since 2007).
items.markingKey: A claim is the position being argued ("the voting age should be 16"); evidence is the support for it (Austria's experience since 2007). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: "Opinion columns do not need evidence because they are opinions." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Effective columns support opinions with evidence, examples and reasoning to persuade readers.

items.stem:
Read the following opinion column by a Year 10 student in a school magazine in Melbourne.

Why I've Changed My Mind About Uniforms
In Year 7 I thought school uniform was a prison sentence in polyester. I wanted to wear my own clothes, my own style, my own identity.
Then I met Jonah. Jonah's family couldn't afford the brands everyone else wore. On mufti days he 'forgot' and wore his blazer anyway.
A uniform doesn't erase who we are. It erases the price tag.
Yes, the jumpers are itchy. Yes, the colour is a crime against fashion. But I'd rather be itchy than watch a friend hide.

Identify the rhetorical appeal used in "Yes, the jumpers are itchy." and explain its effect.
items.answer: Concession: "Yes, the jumpers are itchy." – admitting the weak points makes the writer seem fair and honest, which strengthens the argument.
items.markingKey: Concession: "Yes, the jumpers are itchy." – admitting the weak points makes the writer seem fair and honest, which strengthens the argument. Naming a feature without explaining its effect: half marks at most.

items.stem:
Read the following letter from a student to her local council in Manchester.

Dear Councillor Patel,
I am writing to ask you to reconsider the decision to close Levenshulme Library.
For many students in my area, the library is the only quiet place to study. My flat has five people and one table. The library has Wi-Fi, printers and Mrs Okafor, who has helped me with every homework project since I was eight.
Closing it would save money this year, but it would cost our community far more in the future.
I would be grateful if you could meet our youth group to discuss alternatives.
Yours sincerely,
Amira Hassan (age 14)

Identify the intended audience of this letter. Support your answer with one reference to the text.
items.answer: A local councillor who has power over the decision; the formal salutation and polite requests suit this official audience. Supporting evidence: "I would be grateful if you could meet our youth group" (formal register) – polite, formal language shows respect and makes the request hard to refuse.
items.markingKey: A local councillor who has power over the decision; the formal salutation and polite requests suit this official audience. Supporting evidence: "I would be grateful if you could meet our youth group" (formal register) – polite, formal language shows respect and makes the request hard to refuse. Award marks for an accurate, specific point supported by a reference to the text (criterion A). A general assertion without evidence earns at most 1 mark.

Answer the following question in a well-organised response of about 250 words: How does the writer persuade readers to change their minds about school uniform?
items.answer: The writer first agrees with the reader ("a prison sentence in polyester"), building trust through humour. The anecdote about Jonah and the scare quotes around "forgot" create sympathy and reveal hidden inequality. The antithesis "It doesn't erase who we are. It erases the price tag" reframes the debate, and the concessions ("Yes, the jumpers are itchy") make the writer seem fair before the emotional final line.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "Logos is the most important rhetorical appeal."
items.answer: Logos is essential, but its impact depends on the speaker's credibility and on emotional engagement; the appeals work best together.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: evidence makes an argument credible; it withstands scrutiny. Arguments against: audiences act on emotion; without ethos the evidence may not be trusted. Supported judgement: Logos is essential, but its impact depends on the speaker's credibility and on emotional engagement; the appeals work best together. B Organising: a clear, logical structure suited to the task; ideas linked with purpose; referencing conventions. C Producing text: insight, imagination and personal engagement; deliberate stylistic choices; relevant detail and examples. D Using language: varied, accurate vocabulary, sentence structures and forms of expression; appropriate register and style; accurate grammar, spelling and punctuation. 7-8 perceptive/excellent; 5-6 substantial; 3-4 adequate; 1-2 limited.

items.stem: "Humour makes an opinion column more persuasive." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: Humour can be very persuasive when it supports, rather than replaces, a serious argument, as in the uniform column.
